paragraphs.heading: Burning fuel inside the engine
paragraphs.text: An internal combustion engine is a heat engine that burns its fuel inside itself. The fuel burns with an oxidizer, most often air, inside a chamber that is built into the route the working fluid takes. The burning makes gases that are very hot and under high pressure. As those gases expand, they push directly on parts of the engine.

paragraphs.heading: From push to motion
paragraphs.text: What gets pushed depends on the design: pistons in a piston engine, blades in a gas turbine, a rotor in a Wankel engine, or a nozzle in a jet engine. The push moves that part through a distance. In this way chemical energy stored in the fuel becomes energy of motion. That motion drives, propels or powers whatever the engine is connected to.

paragraphs.heading: Two families
paragraphs.text: Most often the name means an engine where burning happens in separate bursts, like the familiar two-stroke and four-stroke piston engines and the Wankel rotary engine. A second group burns fuel without stopping: gas turbines, jet engines and most rocket engines work this way on the same basic idea. Compare this with an external combustion engine, such as a steam or Stirling engine. There the energy reaches a working fluid that never mixes with the products of burning.

paragraphs.heading: Where they are used
paragraphs.text: Some of these engines sit still, but most are built to move, and they are the main power source for cars, aircraft and boats. Piston engines that move back and forth are by far the most common power for vehicles on land and water, including motorcycles and ships. Most run on fuels made of hydrocarbons, such as natural gas, gasoline, diesel or ethanol. Renewable fuels such as biodiesel are used as well, and renewable fuels are often mixed in with fossil ones.

paragraphs.heading: A long line of inventors
paragraphs.text: Many scientists and engineers had a hand in these engines. John Barber developed the gas turbine in 1791, and in 1807 the French engineers Nicéphore and Claude Niépce ran an early engine on controlled dust explosions that drove a boat on the Saône river. Belgian engineer Jean Joseph Etienne Lenoir made a gas-fired engine in 1860. The first engines to succeed commercially appeared in the middle of the 19th century.

paragraphs.heading: Otto, Benz and Diesel
paragraphs.text: The German engineer Nicolaus Otto designed the first modern internal combustion engine in 1876. Working with Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach, he patented the four-cycle engine with a compressed charge. In 1886 Benz started the first commercial production of motor vehicles powered this way. Rudolf Diesel developed the first compression ignition engine with a compressed charge in 1892, and by 1900 he was running his engines on peanut oil.
